sqlModules.title: Db2 for i foundations
sqlModules.summary: Understand schemas, tables, rows, columns, keys, nulls, and the difference between a statement and a transaction.
points: A table is a set of rows described by columns; a physical file can be used through SQL, but a logical file is not the same thing as a SQL view.
Use a qualified name such as MYLIB.CUSTOMER so a library-list change cannot silently select another object.
A primary key expresses identity. A unique constraint enforces a rule. An index supports access; it does not replace a business rule.
sqlModules.code:
SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, NAME
  FROM MYLIB.CUSTOMER
 WHERE STATUS = 'A'
 ORDER BY CUSTOMER_ID;

sources.title: IBM: Db2 for i SQL programming
IBM: Db2 for i SQL reference

sqlModules.title: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
sqlModules.summary: Write safe data-changing statements and explain the row set or predicate before executing them.
points: SELECT should name the columns needed by the caller. Avoid SELECT * in stable interfaces because schema changes can change the result contract.
INSERT should name its target columns. UPDATE and DELETE need a deliberate WHERE predicate and a row-count check.
Use parameter markers from the application rather than concatenating user input into SQL text.
sqlModules.code:
-- Preview the exact rows before changing them
SELECT ORDER_ID, STATUS
  FROM MYLIB.ORDERS
 WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId;

UPDATE MYLIB.ORDERS
   SET STATUS = :newStatus
 WHERE ORDER_ID = :orderId;

sqlModules.title: Joins, grouping, and subqueries
sqlModules.summary: Combine related tables while preserving the intended cardinality and handling missing related rows.
points: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN keeps the left row and produces nulls when the right side is absent.
Put filters on the correct side of an outer join; a WHERE predicate on the right table can turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner result.
GROUP BY creates one row per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before aggregation.
sqlModules.code:
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID, c.NAME, COUNT(o.ORDER_ID) AS ORDER_COUNT
  FROM MYLIB.CUSTOMER AS c
  LEFT JOIN MYLIB.ORDERS AS o
    ON o.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
 GROUP BY c.CUSTOMER_ID, c.NAME
HAVING COUNT(o.ORDER_ID) > 0;

sqlModules.title: Views and reusable query contracts
sqlModules.summary: Use views to expose a stable, permission-aware shape without copying data.
points: A view stores a query definition. It normally does not store a second copy of the table rows.
Use a view to hide joins, expose only approved columns, or give reporting consumers a stable name.
Document whether a view is intended for reading only and test how inserts or updates behave before allowing them.

sqlModules.title: Variables, indicators, and cursors
sqlModules.summary: Move values safely between SQL and RPG, and process multi-row results without stale data.
points: A host variable is an RPG variable referenced by a colon in embedded SQL.
A nullable column needs a null indicator or a nullable host structure; do not confuse NULL with zero or blank.
A cursor has a lifecycle: DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, handle end-of-data, then CLOSE. A singleton SELECT is not a substitute for a cursor when multiple rows are expected.

sources.title: IBM: Using host variables in ILE RPG applications
IBM: Cursors in ILE RPG applications

sqlModules.title: Transactions, isolation, and performance
sqlModules.summary: Make changes atomic, understand locks, and measure access paths before changing indexes or SQL.
points: Commitment control groups related changes into a unit that can commit or roll back together.
Isolation affects what a transaction can see and how it locks data. Choose it from the consistency requirement, not from habit.
When a statement slows down, capture the statement, row counts, access plan, waits, and timing. An index change without measurement can make another workload worse.

fileOps.meaning: Read the next sequential record from the current file position.
fileOps.example:
read CUSTOMER;
if not %eof(CUSTOMER); // use the record

fileOps.meaning: Retrieve one record by key or relative record number.
fileOps.example:
chain customerId CUSTOMER;
if %found(CUSTOMER); // use the record

fileOps.meaning: Position at the first record greater than or equal to a key; %EQUAL tells you whether the key exists.
fileOps.example:
setll customerId CUSTOMER;
if %equal(CUSTOMER); // exact key exists
fileOps.sql: SELECT ... WHERE CUSTOMER_ID >= :customerId ORDER BY CUSTOMER_ID FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY

fileOps.meaning: Position after a key so a following READP can retrieve the prior record.
fileOps.sql: SELECT ... WHERE CUSTOMER_ID < :customerId ORDER BY CUSTOMER_ID DESC FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY

fileOps.meaning: Read the next record while its key remains equal to the search key.
fileOps.example:
setll customerId ORDER;
reade customerId ORDER;
fileOps.sql: SELECT ... WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId ORDER BY key

fileOps.meaning: Read the previous record relative to the current file position.
fileOps.sql: SELECT ... WHERE key < :currentKey ORDER BY key DESC FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY

fileOps.meaning: Read the previous record whose key equals the search key.
fileOps.sql: SELECT ... WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId AND key < :currentKey ORDER BY key DESC FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY

fileOps.meaning: Create a new record in an output-capable file.
Modify the most recently read record that is eligible for update.
fileOps.example:
chain orderId ORDER;
if %found(ORDER); update ORDER;

fileOps.meaning: Delete the current eligible record or a record found by key.
fileOps.example:
chain orderId ORDER;
if %found(ORDER); delete ORDER;

fileOps.meaning: Write a display format and wait for input in one operation.
fileOps.sql: No direct SQL equivalent; use a UI boundary around the database operation

fileOps.meaning: Read the next changed subfile record.
fileOps.example:
readc SFLREC;
if not %eof(); // validate changed row
fileOps.sql: No direct SQL equivalent; changed-row state belongs to the display program

fileOps.meaning: Explicitly open or close a file when USROPN or resource ownership requires it.
fileOps.sql: Connection and cursor lifecycle are the closest SQL analogue

fileOps.meaning: Commit or roll back the current transaction when commitment control is active.

comparisons.sql: SELECT * FROM MYLIB.CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId
comparisons.note: CHAIN returns a record buffer and %FOUND; SQL returns a result row and SQLSTATE. Both need a not-found branch.

comparisons.sql: SELECT 1 FROM MYLIB.MYFILE WHERE KEY = :key FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
comparisons.note: SETLL can be a cheaper existence check than CHAIN in suitable RPG access paths. SQL still needs a deliberate index and plan.

comparisons.rpg: SETLL customerId ORDER; READE customerId ORDER
comparisons.sql: SELECT * FROM MYLIB.ORDER WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId ORDER BY ORDER_ID
comparisons.note: READE stops at the equal-key boundary; SQL expresses the whole row set. Always define ordering when the application depends on it.

comparisons.sql: SELECT ... FROM MYLIB.MYFILE ORDER BY key
comparisons.note: RPG uses a file cursor and EOF status; SQL uses a cursor and SQLSTATE 02000. Do not process stale host variables after end-of-data.

comparisons.sql: INSERT INTO MYLIB.MYFILE (...) VALUES (...)
comparisons.note: Both can fail on duplicate keys or constraints. Handle the failure and preserve the diagnostic.

comparisons.sql: UPDATE MYLIB.MYFILE SET ... WHERE KEY = :key
comparisons.note: RPG update depends on the current record and lock state; SQL should make the predicate and optimistic version check explicit.

comparisons.sql: DELETE FROM MYLIB.MYFILE WHERE KEY = :key
comparisons.note: Preview the predicate and check affected-row count. A missing key is different from a successful delete.

comparisons.sql: SELECT ... WHERE key < :key ORDER BY key DESC FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
comparisons.note: The SQL ordering and strict less-than boundary must match the RPG cursor intent.

comparisons.sql: SELECT ... WHERE key = :key; inspect SQLSTATE and diagnostics
comparisons.note: The RPG E extender routes an operation exception to program status handling; SQL must check SQLSTATE and preserve diagnostic details.

comparisons.sql: SELECT ... FOR READ ONLY
comparisons.when: Read without holding an update lock
comparisons.note: The exact lock behavior depends on file and isolation settings. Treat both as read intent and revalidate before a later update.

comparisons.sql: UPDATE MYLIB.MYFILE SET ... WHERE key = :key AND version = :version
comparisons.note: SQL makes the version predicate explicit. RPG must compare a refreshed record or version before writing to avoid overwriting a concurrent change.

comparisons.sql: SELECT staged rows WHERE changed_by = :user
comparisons.note: READC is a display-file state operation. SQL can persist staged edits, but it cannot replace the workstation change indicator.

comparisons.sql: INSERT header; INSERT detail; COMMIT
comparisons.when: Create a header with detail rows
comparisons.note: Both patterns need one transaction boundary and a rollback path so a partial order is not left behind.

comparisons.sql: ORDER BY key DESC OFFSET :skip ROWS FETCH NEXT :page ROWS ONLY
comparisons.note: Keyset paging is often more stable than OFFSET for changing data; choose the method after measuring the workload and defining a stable order.

comparisons.sql: WHERE region = :region AND warehouse = :warehouse ORDER BY sku
comparisons.note: Both depend on key field order and compatible values. Verify the access path and boundary semantics before assuming identical results.

comparisons.sql: DELETE FROM MYLIB.MYFILE WHERE key = :key AND status = 'C'
comparisons.note: Make the business condition part of the final predicate or revalidate under the appropriate lock; a prior read alone can become stale.

comparisons.when: One keyed customer lookup with a not-found branch
comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: Both shapes represent a zero-or-one-row contract. CHAIN reports %FOUND; the SQL singleton SELECT reports SQLSTATE 02000 for no row. Neither branch should use fields left over from a prior read.

comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: Use an existence check only when you do not need the record fields. A subsequent change still needs its own final predicate or lock/concurrency policy.

comparisons.when: Read every order for one customer
comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: READE stops automatically at the equal-key boundary. In SQL, the WHERE predicate defines that boundary and ORDER BY defines the processing order. A full cursor loop must test SQLSTATE after each FETCH.

comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: The native record format and SQL result format are different, but both need a clear start, end, stable ordering, and a clean end-of-data branch.

comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: WRITE and INSERT both create a row. SQL lets the target columns and constraints be visible in the statement; native I/O writes the populated record buffer. In both cases, keep the duplicate/error branch explicit.

comparisons.when: Change a row only when its version is current
comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.sql:
**free
exec sql
  update MYLIB.ORDERS
     set STATUS = 'COMPLETE',
         VERSION = VERSION + 1
   where ORDER_ID = :orderId
     and VERSION = :expectedVersion;

// A zero-row result means stale or missing data.
comparisons.note: Both approaches need a concurrency decision. SQL expresses the final version test in the update predicate; native I/O must avoid overwriting a row that changed after it was read.

comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.note: Put the business condition in the final SQL predicate. In native I/O, recheck the record state immediately before DELETE and account for the chosen locking or commitment-control behavior.

comparisons.when: Read an order with optional shipment data
comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.sql:
**free
exec sql
  select o.TOTAL, s.SHIPPED_DATE
    into :orderTotal, :shippedDate :shippedDateNull
    from MYLIB.ORDERS o
    left join MYLIB.SHIPMENT s
      on s.ORDER_ID = o.ORDER_ID
   where o.ORDER_ID = :orderId;
comparisons.note: Nested CHAIN calls are procedural and can be fine for a single request. A LEFT JOIN states the relationship in one query and uses a null indicator when the optional shipment does not exist.

comparisons.when: Calculate an aggregate instead of looping to add totals
comparisons.sqlLabel: Fully free RPGLE with embedded SQL
comparisons.sql:
**free
exec sql
  select coalesce(sum(AMOUNT), 0)
    into :totalAmount
    from MYLIB.ORDERS
   where CUSTOMER_ID = :customerId;
comparisons.note: For a straightforward aggregate, let Db2 do the addition in one statement. Use the RPG loop only when every row has procedural work that cannot be expressed safely in SQL.

rpgleGuide.title: SQL control options and compile intent
rpgleGuide.summary: Set the SQL naming, commitment, date, and error-handling choices deliberately before writing statements.
points: SQL precompiler options such as COMMIT, NAMING, CLOSQLCSR, and DATFMT affect how embedded SQL is interpreted and how resources behave. Confirm the option names and release defaults in the IBM reference for your build command.
Use a qualified naming strategy when a program must not depend on a changing library list. Keep compile options with the source and build record.
Choose *NONE or a commitment-control level from the transaction requirement; do not enable a mode without understanding journaling and rollback expectations.

rpgleGuide.title: Read one row into RPG host variables
rpgleGuide.summary: Use a singleton SELECT when the predicate is intended to return zero or one row.
points: Declare RPG variables with types that match the SQL columns and prefix them with a colon in embedded SQL.
Handle SQLSTATE 02000 before using the target variables. A no-row result must not leave the previous customer in the output fields.
If several rows are valid, use a cursor or multi-row fetch rather than hiding the cardinality error.

rpgleGuide.title: Read a file with a cursor loop
rpgleGuide.summary: Declare, open, fetch, test end-of-data, and close in a predictable lifecycle.
points: The cursor query should have a stable ORDER BY when the program depends on processing order.
After each FETCH, check SQLSTATE or the SQL communication area before processing host variables.
Close the cursor in normal and error cleanup paths. Keep the loop bounded or observable for batch workloads.

rpgleGuide.title: Insert, update, and delete from RPGLE
rpgleGuide.summary: Use parameterized values and make affected-row expectations explicit.
points: Name target columns in INSERT statements and bind values rather than concatenating text.
After UPDATE or DELETE, check the expected row count and distinguish zero rows from a successful change.
For a duplicate or constraint error, preserve the SQLSTATE and message text so the caller can choose a business response.

rpgleGuide.title: Nullable columns and indicator variables
rpgleGuide.summary: Keep NULL, zero, blank, and not-found as separate states.
points: A null-capable result needs a null indicator or an equivalent nullable host structure.
Check the indicator before formatting or calculating with the host variable.
If the application needs a default, make that conversion explicit in SQL with COALESCE or in RPG after the null state is known.

rpgleGuide.title: Commit, rollback, and error cleanup
rpgleGuide.summary: Group related changes and leave the database in a known state after failure.
points: Make the transaction boundary visible: begin or use the configured commitment scope, perform related statements, then commit once the checks pass.
On a handled failure, roll back the unit and return the original diagnostic. Do not commit a marker separately from the business update when replay is possible.
Test the failure between statements and after a process interruption, not only the happy path.

rpgleGuide.title: Calling stored procedures and SQL routines
rpgleGuide.summary: Treat a routine call as an interface with typed inputs, outputs, and diagnostics.
points: Document parameter order, data types, nullability, and expected SQLSTATE values at the RPG boundary.
Use host variables for IN, OUT, and INOUT values and validate outputs before using them.
Keep authorization and transaction behavior explicit; a routine can participate in the caller's transaction.

rpgleGuide.title: Set-based SQL versus RPG row loops
rpgleGuide.summary: Choose whether the database or the RPG program should own the work.
points: A set-based UPDATE or aggregate can avoid moving every row through RPG, but it must have a reviewed predicate and measured plan.
Use an RPG loop when each row needs procedural validation, external calls, or a detailed recovery path.
When mixing the two, define the transaction, ordering, restart marker, and idempotency behavior.

rpgleGuide.title: Keyed lookup: CHAIN thinking with SELECT INTO
rpgleGuide.summary: Use a singleton SELECT for a business key that should return zero or one row, then branch before using host variables.
points: The colon prefixes RPG host variables. The SQL statement stays parameterized; do not build the key into SQL text.
SQLSTATE 02000 is the normal not-found branch. It is not a successful row read.
If duplicate rows are possible, repair the data rule or use a cursor; do not hide an unexpected many-row result.

rpgleGuide.title: Existence check without fetching the row
rpgleGuide.summary: Ask the database whether a row exists when the program does not need the record fields.
points: This is the embedded SQL equivalent of a lightweight SETLL/%EQUAL-style existence decision, not a replacement for a later validated update.
Use FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY so the statement expresses that one answer is sufficient.
A later UPDATE must still include its business condition because another job can change the row after this check.

rpgleGuide.title: Read all equal-key rows with a cursor
rpgleGuide.summary: Use a cursor when a customer can own many order rows and the RPG procedure must process each one.
points: The WHERE predicate represents READE's equal-key boundary; ORDER BY makes the processing order explicit.
FETCH writes into host variables. Process them only after SQLSTATE 00000, and exit on 02000.
Always close the cursor, including on an error path, so the program does not retain cursor resources longer than intended.

rpgleGuide.title: Read the next ordered page
rpgleGuide.summary: Use a stable order and keyset boundary when the program needs the next small group of rows.
points: A predicate such as ORDER_ID > :lastOrderId describes the boundary explicitly, unlike relying on an earlier cursor position in another call.
FETCH FIRST limits the result set. The program can move the boundary only after it has successfully processed each row.
For changing data, keyset paging is often easier to reason about than a large OFFSET, but choose after measuring the real workload.

rpgleGuide.title: Join tables instead of nested file reads
rpgleGuide.summary: Let Db2 match related rows when the procedure needs columns from multiple files or tables.
points: A LEFT JOIN keeps an order even when its optional shipment row is absent. Use a null indicator for nullable right-side columns.
Name the columns and qualify them with aliases so a later schema change or join does not make the result ambiguous.
If the business request needs many result rows, move this SELECT into a cursor rather than assuming one order is returned.

rpgleGuide.title: Update and delete with a final business predicate
rpgleGuide.summary: Make the change condition visible in the SQL statement so the row is not changed merely because it was read earlier.
points: The version or status predicate is an optimistic-concurrency check. A zero-row update is a business outcome that needs a deliberate branch.
Use one transaction for related header, detail, and status changes. Do not commit a partial business action.
For DELETE, add the required status or ownership condition rather than deleting solely by key when the rule depends on current state.

rpgleGuide.title: Use a CTE when the business step has a name
rpgleGuide.summary: A common table expression makes a multi-step query readable without creating a permanent table or view.
points: WITH creates a result name for the one SQL statement. It is useful when an aggregate, filter, or join needs to be understood before the final SELECT.
A CTE is not a promise that Db2 materializes a temporary table; the optimizer chooses how to execute the statement.
In RPGLE, a singleton final SELECT still needs the zero-row and error branches shown in the earlier examples.

errors.name: SQLSTATE 02000 / %EOF
errors.meaning: No row or end of data
errors.action: Branch before using host variables or record fields; do not process the previous row again.

errors.name: SQLSTATE 23505 / duplicate key
errors.meaning: A unique rule rejected the insert or update
errors.action: Decide whether this is an expected business conflict or an application defect; do not blindly retry.

errors.name: SQL7008
errors.meaning: The object is not valid for the requested SQL operation; the reason detail matters
errors.action: Read the complete diagnostic, then inspect journaling, commitment control, object type, and authority for that reason.

errors.name: RPG status 1218 / record in use
errors.meaning: A record is locked by another job
errors.action: Inspect the holder, use a bounded retry only when safe, and re-read before updating.

errors.name: RPG %FOUND false or %EOF true
errors.meaning: The keyed read did not find a row or the scan reached its boundary
errors.action: Handle the branch explicitly and reset/reposition before trying another scan.

errors.name: CPF4131 / level check
errors.meaning: The compiled file format does not match the file being opened
errors.action: Identify the resolved object and format change, then rebuild or deploy the compatible pair in a controlled sequence.

sqlCodes.when: The database completed the statement without an error or exceptional condition.
sqlCodes.action: Continue. For INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, also verify the affected-row count matches the business expectation.

sqlCodes.meaning: No row found or end of data
sqlCodes.when: A singleton SELECT finds no row, or a FETCH reaches the end of a cursor result.
sqlCodes.action: Treat it as an expected branch when the use case allows it. Clear or initialise output fields so a previous row is not reused.

sqlCodes.meaning: Data conversion or data mapping problem
sqlCodes.when: A value overflows, has an invalid numeric/date format, divides by zero, or cannot be mapped to the target type. The sign determines warning versus error for the returned condition.
sqlCodes.action: Read the job log and diagnostic tokens, identify the failing value and target column or host variable, then correct the data or type conversion.

sqlCodes.meaning: Referenced object or name is not found
sqlCodes.when: A table, view, alias, routine, function, or other SQL object cannot be resolved in the build or run environment.
sqlCodes.action: Check the qualified library/schema, object type, spelling, library list, and authority. Use the SQL0204 message details rather than guessing.

sqlCodes.meaning: Column is not in the table or view
sqlCodes.when: The statement names a column that does not exist, was renamed, or is ambiguous after a schema change.
sqlCodes.action: Verify the column in the catalog, qualify columns when joining tables, and re-precompile or rebuild the program after a schema change.

sqlCodes.meaning: Host variable is incompatible or too small
sqlCodes.when: A FETCH, SELECT, CALL, or assignment cannot map the SQL value to the RPG or host variable type or length.
sqlCodes.action: Compare SQL column and host-variable types, lengths, precision, and date formats. Correct the definition before retrying.

sqlCodes.when: A nullable result is assigned to a host variable without an indicator or nullable host structure.
sqlCodes.action: Add an indicator and branch on its negative value, or use an explicit COALESCE only when replacing NULL has the intended business meaning.

sqlCodes.meaning: NULL cannot be stored in a NOT NULL column
sqlCodes.when: An INSERT or UPDATE supplies NULL, or omits a required column without a default.
sqlCodes.action: Supply a valid value or deliberate default, or change the nullable design. Do not silently convert an unknown value to blank or zero.

sqlCodes.meaning: Foreign-key value has no matching parent
sqlCodes.when: A child row is inserted or updated before its referenced parent row exists.
sqlCodes.action: Check the parent key and constraint definition, and insert or correct the parent in the same controlled transaction when appropriate.

sqlCodes.meaning: Parent row cannot be deleted because dependents exist
sqlCodes.when: A DELETE or key change violates a RESTRICT or NO ACTION referential rule.
sqlCodes.action: Find dependent rows and follow the documented business delete order. Never remove a constraint just to make the statement pass.

sqlCodes.meaning: User is not authorised for the object or operation
sqlCodes.when: The job profile lacks the required authority on a table, view, routine, package, or underlying file.
sqlCodes.action: Identify the exact object and required privilege, then request the narrow authority from the owner or security administrator.

sqlCodes.meaning: Duplicate key or unique constraint violation
sqlCodes.when: An INSERT or UPDATE would create a duplicate value in a primary key, unique constraint, or unique index.
sqlCodes.action: Decide whether the conflict is an expected business response or a defect. Inspect the key and transaction before retrying.

sqlCodes.meaning: A singleton SELECT returned more than one row
sqlCodes.when: SELECT INTO or a scalar subquery is used where the data matches multiple rows.
sqlCodes.action: Fix the predicate or data rule if one row is required; otherwise use a cursor, multi-row fetch, or an intentional aggregate.

sqlCodes.meaning: Row or object is in use after a deadlock or timeout
sqlCodes.when: The requested row or object remains locked beyond the configured wait time or a deadlock is detected.
sqlCodes.action: Read the preceding messages, inspect locks, keep transactions short, and retry only when the operation is idempotent and the retry policy is bounded.
sqlCodes.example: // Review DSPRCDLCK or WRKOBJLCK evidence before changing retry logic

sqlCodes.meaning: SQL processing ended before normal completion
sqlCodes.when: A client cancellation, abnormal termination, activation-group end, or another interruption stops SQL processing.
sqlCodes.action: Read the preceding job-log messages and reason code. Roll back or clean up as required; do not treat cancellation as a no-data result.
